The novel thing about quantum computing isn't really that it may or may not run "faster" than normal computers in an instruction-by-instruction way, but that it can run algorithms normal computers can not, like, Shor's algorithm, which will break RSA encryption by lowering the prime factorization problem to polynomial difficulty. So even if there's a speed limit that makes quantum computers even a million times slower than normal computers at general purpose computing, they'll still be hugely faster doing things where there are quantum algorithms that are in a lower class of difficulty than the best conventional algorithm. TL;DR even if quantum computers are too slow to ever be useful running web browsers or farmville, once they're up to enough bits, most modern encryption is still toast.

Theoretically (I've posted a few links before), there should be no major issues with encryption - so long as we upgrade our encryption to the new techniques.

And, yeah... A common misconception is that a quantum computer is faster. No, they aren't. What they are good at is having more than two states - of just off an on.
